idiom_name: #cell?: T plus get accessor returning a non-nullable T
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime, so the realization is the JavaScript guard and the type system's job is to keep the marker internal: the cell is typed as optional/undefined inside the class while the accessor's declared return type is non-nullable, so callers never handle 'not built yet' and cannot forget a null check. Logical assignment operators (??=, ||=, &&=) are supported from TypeScript 4.0 and downlevelled according to target. The classic explicit isInitialized flag survives only where undefined is a legitimate value or where the cell must be reset; async laziness is typed as a cached Promise<T>, not as T.
pitfalls: `#report?: Report` plus ??= conflates 'not built' with 'built to undefined': when the value can legitimately be undefined, model the cell as { built: boolean; value?: T } or use a Lazy<T | undefined> accessor explicitly.
Declaring the cell as T and asserting non-null (!) at the use site type-checks but removes exactly the guarantee the accessor was supposed to provide.

With older targets (ES2019 and below) TS downlevels ??= into a read-then-write sequence, so the atomicity of the compiled form differs from the modern operator - check the emitted code when the cell is shared.
Type-level laziness is a fiction: `readonly report: Report` on the class field makes it look eagerly built even when the getter defers, so the API shape hides the first-access cost.

variants.name: Cached-promise cell for async initialisation
variants.idiom_name: private pending?: Promise<T> with a memoised accessor
variants.implementation_notes: Asynchronous initialisation cannot be a getter: the accessor is async and memoises the promise itself, so concurrent callers awaiting the same accessor share one in-flight initialisation instead of racing. Typing the cell as Promise<T> (never T) is what makes the sharing visible - a common bug is caching the resolved value and therefore starting a second load on every concurrent access. This variant replaces the sync guard for cases like lazily fetched tokens, remote schema or connection pools.
pitfalls: Caching the awaited value rather than the promise lets two callers both start the work; the promise cell must be assigned synchronously, before the first await.
A rejected promise stays cached: unless the catch resets the cell, a transient network failure becomes permanent - decide the retry policy explicitly.
An unhandled rejection in the cached promise is easy to create (nobody awaits the same promise) and surfaces as an unhandledRejection long before a caller sees it.

variants.name: Memoising accessor decorator
variants.implementation_notes: With standard (TS 5) decorators the laziness can be declared instead of written: an accessor decorator wraps the builder so the first access caches its result on the instance, which replaces the manual cell entirely for class members and keeps the guard in one reusable function. It is the right variant when many members across a codebase are lazily built and the team wants one audited implementation; it is the wrong one when the project still uses experimental decorators or relies on class-field initialisation order, because both change when the decorator runs.
pitfalls: Decorator flavours are not interchangeable: experimentalDecorators/emitDecoratorMetadata produce different runtime semantics from the TS 5 standard decorators, and a library written for one silently misbehaves with the other.
Decorating a field instead of an accessor runs the initialiser at construction time, giving eager semantics with lazy-looking syntax.

The cache lives on the instance (usually a weak map or a hidden property), so it can keep values alive longer than expected and is invisible in the class's declared members; provide a reset for mutable dependencies.
